Himalayas face severe glacial flood risks in years ahead, UN official warns

The Himalayan region faces severe risks from future glacial floods, an assistant secretary-general at the UN has warned.

The Nepal-Tibet floods have overrun hydropower facilities, knocking out about 10% of Nepal’s power capacity. There are now fears that entire riverbanks where millions of people live might become ⁠effectively uninhabitable.

“Technology cannot move fast enough to prevent loss along these massive river systems that catch the overflow of the glacier lakes,” Kanni Wignaraja told the Reuters news agency.

Researchers identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal, China and India in 2020 – but the real figure is now thought to be significantly higher.

The population at risk “goes into ‌the millions”, Wignaraja said, citing updated data compiled by the United Nations Development Programme and partner organisations in June.

Last week’s catastrophic flooding was triggered when parts of a glacier near the Langtang Lirung mountain peak collapsed and fell to the valley floor, unleashing a landslide that sent a flood wave down the Trishuli River.

Glacier lake outbursts happen when melting glacier water accumulates behind a natural barrier, with pressure eventually ‌resulting in a break or overflow that sends a flash flood downstream.

Both threats are on the rise, UN officials say, as the climate crisis accelerates glacier melt in the region, loosening ​rocks and putting more pressure on glacier lake barriers.

Closing summary

Devastating floods on the China-Nepal border have killed at least 1,050 people in Nepal, the disaster authority said on Tuesday, with nearly 4,000 more missing. Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 people were killed in Tibet , taking the total toll from Wednesday’s disaster to 1,066.

The Himalayan region faces severe risks from future glacial floods, an assistant secretary-general at the UN has warned. The Nepal-Tibet floods have overrun hydropower facilities, knocking out about 10% of Nepal’s power capacity. There are now fears that entire riverbanks where millions of people live might become ⁠effectively uninhabitable.

Researchers identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal, China and India in 2020 – but the real figure is now thought to be significantly higher. The population at risk “goes into ‌the millions”, Wignaraja said, citing updated data compiled by the United Nations Development Programme and partner organisations in June.

The disaster has left at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, according to a preliminary estimate by the United Nations Development ​Programme (UNDP), including parts of buildings, rocks, and sediment. “The amount of debris shows the scale ‌of the destruction and the challenge communities face ‌as they clear homes, roads and public spaces and begin to rebuild,” it said.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada. Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

Nepal last week turned down foreign ​involvement in general search and rescue but said it needed specialised services and advanced technological support in areas such as life-detecting machines, large refrigerators and prefabricated bridges. Aid worth more than $42m has poured into the country and Nepal is now working with experts from other countries to help with rescue operations.

In the capital Kathmandu, crowds lined up to search for their missing relatives, posting photographs on a long wall outside a hospital in the fading hope of finding them alive. Debu Sapkota, a 58-year-old driver, came to post photos of his 83-year-old mother-in-law and her granddaughter who went missing in the town of Trishuli Bazaar after being swept away by last week’s surge.

Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah said that the disaster highlighted the need for action to combat the climate crisis. “This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change,” Shah said in a social media post on Monday night.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China’s second batch of relief supplies for Nepal was expected to ship today, including drones, DNA testing and water purification equipment. Chinese DNA testing experts will also help Nepal identity bodies, he said. Beijing has said it will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.

Three months before last week’s devastating floods, experts from China and Nepal met in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, on 27 May to discuss the risk of disasters in the border area and to coordinate on how best to monitor and respond to hazards such as floods, according to the Reuters news agency . The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.

The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions . The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.

Families check a computer database to identify the bodies of their loved ones following a flash flood at a temporary shelter in Chitwan district, Nepal .

Nearly a week after a catastrophic glacier collapse struck the Nepal-China border, the death toll continues to rise as emergency teams search through heavy mud and submerged hydro tunnels. With thousands still unaccounted for, including dozens of Australian travellers, international rescue operations are racing against time.

Guardian reporter Cait Kelly speaks to Rafqa Touma from Kathmandu about the devastation on the ground, the search for survivors and what happens next …

The disaster has left at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, according to a preliminary estimate by the United Nations Development ​Programme (UNDP), including parts of buildings, rocks, and sediment.

“The amount of debris shows the scale ‌of the destruction and the challenge communities face ‌as they clear homes, roads and public spaces and begin to rebuild,” it said.

UK prime minister Andy Burnham pledged to “meet the climate challenge”, as he said Britain was “doing everything” to support Nepal .

In his first appearance as prime minister in the House of Commons, he said: “I know I also speak for the whole House in expressing my profound shock and horror at the devastating scenes on the Nepal-China border.

“My sympathies are with all those affected, including the families and loved ones of those missing in this appalling tragedy. The foreign secretary is doing everything he can to support the Nepalese government and British nationals in the region.

“This is what the climate crisis looks like. We have just ourselves experienced what is likely to have been the hottest summer on record. This government will meet the climate challenge, and I can confirm to the House that I will attend Cop 31 in Turkey in November.”

Nepal says flood death toll rises to 1,050, with total killed now 1,066

Devastating floods on the China-Nepal border have killed at least 1,050 people in Nepal, the disaster authority said on Tuesday, with nearly 4,000 more missing.

Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 people were killed in Tibet , taking the total toll from Wednesday’s disaster to 1,066.

The first slider shows the stark difference in the landscape between 12 August and 27 August – the day after the disaster, caused by a glacial collapse, struck the Tibet-Nepal border.

A second set of images shows the glacier itself before and after the collapse.

Researchers identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal, China and India in 2020 – but the real figure is now thought to be significantly higher.

The population at risk “goes into ‌the millions”, Wignaraja said, citing updated data compiled by the United Nations Development Programme and partner organisations in June.

Last week’s catastrophic flooding was triggered when parts of a glacier near the Langtang Lirung mountain peak collapsed and fell to the valley floor, unleashing a landslide that sent a flood wave down the Trishuli River.

Both threats are on the rise, UN officials say, as the climate crisis accelerates glacier melt in the region, loosening ​rocks and putting more pressure on glacier lake barriers.

In a relief response situation report published today, Nepal’s disaster risk reduction and management authority (NDRRMA) said the majority of deaths – which include recovered human remains – occurred in Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, followed by Nawalparasi East, Nawalparasi West, Nuwakot and Gorkha. The NDRRMA said 1.6 million people were affected from the floods across five districts.

“3,702 households, comprising a population of 14,461 remain isolated in the two most severely affected local levels (Gosaikunda and Amachhodingmo Rural Municipalities, Rasuwa), with road connectivity, electricity, and communication services disrupted for up to six days since the incident, severely limiting access to essential services, supplies, and emergency assistance,” the situation report read.

It said unidentified bodies are being kept at 21 hospitals across various districts, adding that 2,740 people received medical treatment from Nepal’s army following Wednesday’s massive flash food.

In terms of infrastructural impact, the NDRRMA said 41 bridges were washed away in the floods and four bridges damaged, while four health facilities and eight schools were “fully damaged”. In Nepal’s Nuwakot district, 1,267 houses have been reported as “fully damaged” and 1,253 as “partially damaged”.

As police in Kathmandu buried dozens of bodies in multiple trenches, Nepal’s disaster agency said that 1,003 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreign nationals.

The 1,003 figure given here is seven lower than the death toll provided by Nepal’s foreign ministry spokesperson earlier today (see this post ).

In its latest update, China reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including 261 foreigners.

In the capital Kathmandu , crowds lined up to search for their missing relatives, posting photographs on a long wall outside a hospital in the fading hope of finding them alive.

Debu Sapkota, a 58-year-old driver, came to post photos of his 83-year-old mother-in-law and her granddaughter who went missing in the town of Trishuli Bazaar after being swept away by last week’s surge.

A warning alert sounded, but the elderly woman was “too old to run”, he told AP. “Her granddaughter was helping her escape, but both were swept away.”

Sapkota said he no longer has “any hope that they survived”, after witnesses saw them being carried away by the torrent.

“I am here hoping to find their bodies,” he said, holding up photos of the two missing women dressed in traditional clothes.

Here is footage filmed using a drone in the village of Devighat , Nepal , that shows damaged houses and shops, while roads remain covered in thick mud.

Local people have been using heavy machinery to clear the debris-covered streets and rescue efforts are continuing across the country.

“No siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds,” says Prof Anjal Prakash, from Flame University in India. He blames a lack of political will to fight the climate crisis and to plan infrastructure for the devastating flood in Nepal and Tibet .

Prof Prakash said:

double quotation mark Nepal’s mountains have been sending warnings for a decade : thinning glaciers, retreating snowlines, permafrost turning to slush under roads and hydropower plants we kept building anyway . We didn’t lack the science, as researchers have tracked this decline for 50 years. We lacked the political will to act on it . Early warning systems are being sold as the fix, but no siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds . The real failure sits upstream, in land-use decisions that pushed settlements and infrastructure onto riverbanks our ancestors deliberately avoided, and in a global economy still burning the fossil fuels that are cooking these glaciers from the inside out . Every villager who watched that valley disappear paid for emissions decisions made thousands of kilometres away . Until governments treat the Himalayas as a climate frontline rather than a postcard backdrop, Rasuwa won’t be the last name we’re forced to memorise .

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said:

double quotation mark For years, scientists and local communities have been warning that the Hindu Kush Himalayas are at huge risk from climate change. We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe , with vulnerable communities often hardest hit. But the solutions to global heating are equally clear – especially a faster global shift from fossil fuels to renewables and more investment in climate resilience.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues .

At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.

Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.

“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.” You can read more here:

For the record, this is how he sees his record. -Won the Greens’ first ever parliamentary byelection in Gorton and Denton -More than tripled the party membership from 68,500 to over 230,000 Zack Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras sounds like a done deal from the hints the party is dropping over the past 24 hours. stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Burnham offers to work with Tories on getting welfare spending down

Kemi Badenoch starts by congratulating the PM “on his stamina – three hours”. (That generates some laughter.) She asks if Burnham can name a single spending request to which he said no.

Burnham says he was clear about the need to get welfare spending down.

It is not right to have so many young people on benefits. He wants to invest in their success.

This is an area where both parties can engage “in problem solving, not point scoring’.

PMQs - snap verdict

So much for the talk of a new-look PMQs. (See 11.12am .) Although Andy Burnham and his team have spoken about adopting a new approach to the traditional Commons joust with the leader of the opposition, in the end this felt much like business as usual. Burnham was more willing to engage with Kemi Badenoch’s questions than Keir Starmer was (certainly in the late Starmer phase), and he did make a point of stressing several times his desire to work with opposition parties. But, although he has made “problem-solving, not point-scoring” his mantra, Burnham was quite happy to resort to point-scoring. His main blast was directed at Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, and his role in the Liz Truss mini-budget.

Burnham may not have been particularly innovative, but he was good; confident, plausible, quite funny. In the exchanges with Badenoch, there was no obvious winner, but he had the best single put-down. That came when Badenoch asked:

double quotation mark The prime minister told the house that his summer of promises would be paid for by reprioritize within government. So what exactly has he cut?

Burnham replied: “In terms of what has he cut? Tax is the simple answer.” This was a reference to the point he made yesterday about how his early announcements included two tax cuts in his first week.

While Burnham and Badenoch will both be fairly happy with how the exchanges went, one person less pleased will be the PM’s diary secretary. Burnham did seem to agree to a lot of meetings with MPs wanting to discuss this, that or the other. (Starmer would have fobbed them off with a meeting with a minister, which is what Burnham himself will probably be doing before too long.) And this did seem to confirm Badenoch ’s point about Burnham being a people pleaser. (See 12.09pm .) She claimed that, in response to 125 questions yesterday, Burnham did not once say no to a spending request. It is a fair line of attack, although probably not one that will be available for long because Burnham will soon discover that he cannot do this job without having to disappoint.

Just Stop Oil protesters block road outside parliament

Just Stop Oil protesters are blockading the road outside parliament, Kate Ferguson from the Sun on Sunday reports.

Burnham suggests he has committed to getting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030

During PMQs Tan Dhesi , the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, asked Burnham if he would commit to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

He said:

double quotation mark It is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than be sorry later. Indeed, defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough. So rather than kick the can down the road waiting for a fiscal event in the future, will the prime minister urgently commit to charting a pathway to reach 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030, which, as his chancellor rightly noted, is critical to keep our country safe.

John Healey resigned as defence secretary when Keir Starmer was PM because Starmer would not commit to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. He is now chancellor, but has not publicly committed to reaching the 3% target he insisted was essential by 2030.

In reply, Burnham said:

double quotation mark I’ve made that commitment, made it very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time. And I was in Ukraine last week for a very specific reason to repeat it on the world stage. There [Dhesi] can be absolutely sure of that.

This sounded like a clear commitment to 3% by 2030.

But there was some doubt about his intention because earlier during the exchanges, when Kemi Badenoch said that the armed forces needed a plan to hit 3% now, Burnham in reply just repeated the commitment to get defence spending up to 3.5% by 2035. (See 12.18pm .)

Samantha Niblett (Lab) tells Burnham that this is her first question at a PMQs too. Niblett is the MP who made headlines with her “summer of sex” campaign , and she says he has had a tremendous response to it. She says:

double quotation mark I have discovered that shame, guilt and embarrassment around talking about sex and body parts like penis and vagina is even leading to late diagnosis of health conditions and illnesses such as cancer.

She asks if Burnham will meet her to discuss her campaign.

Burnham says he will. He says Niblett has been raising important issues, and he jokes that her summer sounds as if it was more exciting than his.

And that is the end of Burnham’s first PMQs .

Jack Rankin , who has just been appointed as Kemi Badenoch’s PPS , says Burnham did not answer any of Badenoch’s questions. He asks if Burnham can say what the fiscal rules are, and categorically say he will stick to them.

Burnham replies:

double quotation mark No borrowing to fund day to day spending, debt falling as a percentage of GDP by the end of the parliament. And yes, we will.

Danny Kruger (Reform UK) says youth unemployment in Manchester got worse when Burnham was mayor. He says the solution is tax cuts for business.

Burnham says Kruger should look again at the figures. He says he delivered a huge increase in apprenticeships, and Neet numbers went down.

But he offers to work with other parties on youth unemployment.

Helena Dollimore , the Labour MP for Hastings and Rye, welcomes a scheme that will ensure that young people from her constituency get access to the Bayeaux Tapestry exhibition.

Burnham praises Dollimore for her campaigning on this. He says he would like all young people to be able to see the tapestry that they learn about at school.

Andrew George (Lib Dem) asks if Burnham will back his private members’ bill to give local communities more power over housing. He says this is a particularly issue in Cornwall.

Burnham says he will meet George to discuss this.

Burnham says he wants more defence spending going into supporting British industries.

Burnham suggests he is open to devolving power over policing to Welsh government

Liz Saville Roberts , the Plaid Cymru leader at Westminster, asks Burnham to give the Welsh government control over policing.

Burnham says he will give this proposal a fair hearing.

Kim Leadbeater (Lab) asks what Burnham will do to help people suffering from loneliness, or anti-social behaviour.

Burnham thanks Leadbeater for raising these issues. He raised them in the Makerfield byelection, he says. On antisocial behaviour, he says he accepts the broken windows theory – that small acts of criminality should not be ignored.

Bradley Thomas (Con) asks if Burnham will meet him to discuss a new approach to protecting the green belt.

Burnham says as mayor of Greater Manchester he adopted a brownfield first approach. But there is a balance to be struck, he says. He says the Tories should not turn their back on the need for more homes.

Sorcha Eastwood (Alliance) says the Northern Ireland executive cannot function properly under the rules it has to follow (for cross-community government, giving nationalists and unionists in effect a veto over any decisions). She asks if Burnham will reform the situation.

Burnham says he will address this.

double quotation mark Our first responsibility is to get Stormont government up and running and functioning properly with a budget. I’ve empowered the Northern Ireland secretary to go into talks to, to resolve that issue and the broader issues about reform.

Lindsay Hoyle , the Speaker, accepts Burnham is trying to answer questions, but says he is taking too long. At this rate, they won’t get through all the questions, he says,

Burnham says he wants closer relationship with EU - but ducks Lib Dem challenge to back joining single market

Ed Davey , the Lib Dem leader, says Burnham was right yesterday to blame Brexit for the UK’s lack of growth. The answer to the problem is staring us in the face, he says – join the single market.

Burnham says he is glad Davey accepts his analysis. He says he wants a closer relationship with the EU, building on the work of Keir Starmer. The EU’s “Made in Europe” plan could pose real problems for British steelmakers.

Davey says he hopes Burnham will rejoin the single market.

He says in North Devon a maternity unit has been closed, meaning women have to travel two hours to give birth. They are being taught how to give birth in cars. This is “unthinktable”, he says. Will he commit to reopening the maternity unit within days?

Burnham says he will commit to reopening it – but not within days.

He says there are structural problems with maternity units in the country.

stories.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
stories.summary: Higher borrowing costs have piled fresh pressure on Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 September 2026

Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt — a loan to the British government — rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, would be "fiscal responsibility".

Government borrowing, bonds and yields explained Published 14 February 2025

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister , and his Chancellor, John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

The prime minister was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

Burnham's ex-economic adviser Lord Jim O'Neill told BBC News that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to "get real" about "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Lord O'Neill, who recently turned down the offer of a formal position in the prime minister's team, said that current market pressure would force changes over "some of the things that no political figures ever seem to want to deal with".

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

Government spending around the world

Around the world there are warning lights flashing from the markets for government debt.

Global markets reacted in particular after suggestions in the US that its central bank could raise rates. Japan is also facing pressure to raise rates.

The chancellor is in the US attending a meeting of global finance ministers and central bankers. He told the G20 that the UK had the fastest growth in the G7 in 2026 so far, that productivity was improving and that the UK was cutting its borrowing at the fastest rate of the major economies.

US borrowing costs hit a fresh high on Tuesday as renewed strikes in the Middle East pushed up oil prices and heightened concerns over inflation.

Karen Ward, JP Morgan's chief market strategist for Europe, said governments around the world want to increase spending and are turning to borrowing to fund it.

And she told the BBC's World at One they were increasingly having to compete with major technology companies raising money to invest in the AI revolution, pushing up the amount of interest being charged.

"Markets are getting a lot more choice about who they are going to lend to and at what interest rates," she added.

Burnham has rolled out a series of interventions to support consumers and businesses since entering Downing Street, and is expected to prioritise further measures to ease the cost of living in the Budget on 28 October.

Ward urged Burnham and Healey to set out how they will fund any fresh spending on defence and the cost of living, and how those lending the government money will be paid back.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment company XTB, told the BBC News Channel: "Of course, this is red lights flashing."

"We are used to pockets of volatility, it has been volatile few months," she said.

But record levels of government debt and a record tax take mean "these are not comfortable times for the new government and the new chancellor", she added.

Every time bond yields rise, the UK has to pay more on the debt interest, Brooks said.

stories.title: Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services
stories.summary: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians", as he addressed MPs for the first time as PM.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:

This video can not be played

Watch: Key moments from Burnham's first Commons speech as PM

Published 1 September 2026

Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power.

The prime minister said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised and pointed to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".

He reiterated his belief that political power had been centralised and announced he would be making devolution powers available to more areas in England.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong, his theory of growth is completely wrong, he thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said.

Badenoch also warned the prime minister that his new job would be "very different" to his previous Greater Manchester mayoral role where he "did not have to make difficult trade-offs".

Burnham became prime minister on 20 July shortly after Parliament closed for the summer recess.

MPs returned to Parliament on Tuesday providing Burnham with his first opportunity to address the House of Commons and take questions.

He told the chamber that "Britain is not where we would wish it to be", but promised to "build a new sense of optimism around the country".

Following his 10 years away from Parliament, Burnham said he was returning with a "clear diagnosis" of what had gone wrong in the country.

"From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns," he said.

"Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.

"And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."

In the months before becoming prime minister, Burnham stopped short of calling for full nationalisation but said he wanted to see greater public control of water and energy.

On Tuesday, he promised that a plan to achieve this would be produced "later in the year".

Pressed on his plans for the water sector by Conservative MP Alison Griffiths, Burnham said it was important to "look at all possible solutions".

"It's a very regrettable situation that the privatisation of water has left us in a position where we're going to find it very difficult to reverse," he added.

Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament Published 4 days ago

Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to? Published 24 July

Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM Published 18 hours ago

Burnham said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth", namely that devolving powers to regions outside London would boost their economy.

He argued the approach had worked in Manchester and now he wanted "every single place across our regions and nations to be able to do the same, creating the conditions for good growth in every postcode".

Some MPs have raised concern that areas without mayors - and the new powers that have come with them - would suffer, leading to a two-tier system.

Efforts to secure a devolution deal in Cornwall have been stymied by the county's reluctance to form a group with Devon but also to having a mayor.

Burnham appeared to have accepted the county's concerns, telling the House of Commons his government would work with Cornwall Council and its six MPs on a devolution deal "with or without an elected mayor".

He added that he would be extending "the same offer to all parts of England without devolved power".

He also said he was interested in exploring "a local model of devolution" in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Shortly before Burnham's speech to Parliament, Sir Keir Starmer said in a surprise announcement that he would be stepping down as an MP, less than two months after he quit as prime minister.

Burnham began his speech by paying tribute to his predecessor telling the House of Commons that Sir Keir had "given this country a lifetime of public service" and created a "platform to change this country for the better".

In his wide-ranging statement, which lasted three-and-half-hours, Burnham gave an indication of his approach on several other issues including welfare.

He suggested that providing more council homes and thereby bringing down rent for more people would be the "Labour way" of reducing the benefits bill.

The prime minister also committed to introducing legislation that would allow homeowners to move more easily from the leasehold system to a commonhold form of ownership.

Asked by Badenoch about defence spending, Burnham said he had specifically chosen John Healey to be his chancellor because of his "commitment to defence".

Healey resigned as defence secretary earlier this year, accusing then-prime minister Sir Keir of failing to commit the resources needed to keep the country safe.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey used his question to argue that too much power in the UK was in "the wrong hands" and called for "fundamental change" of the political system.

Burnham said he would look at the voting system but would not introduce any changes before the next general election.

Both Reform UK's Richard Tice and the Green Party's Ellie Chowns asked whether the government would approve new drilling licences at the Rosebank oil field and the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

Tice urged the PM to allow more drilling saying it was "madness to import gas from overseas when we have our own gas in the North Sea" while Chowns opposed such a move arguing that the "climate damage they would create hugely outweighs any possible benefit".

Burnham promised to take a "pragmatic approach" and said he wanted the transition to renewable energy to be done "as effectively and affordably as possible".

In-store inflation rises to an annual 1.5% in August, according to a survey for the British Retail Consortium

The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in August, a trade body index shows, with higher energy costs pushing up the price of food and AI chip demand making technology more expensive .

In-store inflation stepped up to 1.5% year on year in August, up from 0.9% in July, led by prices for tinned and packaged food which increased by 2.5% against 1.1% in the prior month, according to data from the research company NIQ for the British Retail Consortium.

Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%, amid pressure on growers from the hot dry summer plus hefty fuel and energy costs. However, that marked a slight easing off from the 3.1% recorded in July,

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the consortium, said: “The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed.

“In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage. Meanwhile, retailers kept clothing prices low to offer value for families getting ready for the new school year.

“The months ahead look challenging for households, with rising bills putting further pressure on budgets.”

Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at NIQ, said he expected price competition between retailers to intensify in the autumn months as businesses competed to attract families concerned about potentially higher energy bills.

However, Dickinson said companies were facing “persistently high operating costs” that limited their ability to absorb price rises. She added: “If the government is serious about supporting growth while keeping the cost of living in check, it must address the cost of doing business, including by tackling the growing burden of business rates, packaging and employment taxes.”

The evidence of higher shop prices comes after the boss of Asda said he was seeing inflation on some fresh food begin to rise after a hot dry summer that affected crop yields.

Cereals including wheat and barley were hit particularly badly, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006.

The rise in shop price inflation adds to the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government in achieving its aim of granting “breathing space” to hard-pressed households

Wider consumer price inflation across the UK rose to 2.9% in July with the Iran war affecting energy prices, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics . The agency said inflation rose from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, driven by more costly gas and electricity.

stories.title: Spaces in male prisons fall to lowest level of year, sources say
stories.summary: Jails in England and Wales are nearing maximum capacity as the justice secretary prepares to give more details in the Commons on the early-release scheme to free inmates.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The early release scheme was launched in September to tackle overcrowding

Published 1 September 2026

The number of available spaces across the male prison estate in England and Wales has fallen to its lowest this year, sources have told the BBC.

As of 1 September, there were about 1,500 free spaces, just under half the number available at the start of June, which Ministry of Justice (MoJ) figures put at 3,040.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the government's early release scheme, which will mean more prisoners, including those convicted of manslaughter, will remain behind bars for longer.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris told the Commons on Tuesday the scheme, which was launched to reduce prison overcrowding, is needed to maintain confidence in British justice.

Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding Published 1 day ago

He also said he will hold some 18-year-olds in young offenders' institutions for longer to delay transferring them to the adult male estate to help with the overcrowding in prisons.

MoJ figures show the number of available male prison spaces has been steadily falling since the middle of June, with the last official figures released on 24 August placing them at 1,665.

This week's numbers have not been officially released due to Monday's bank holiday but prison sources say vacancies have fallen once again.

The government has said it would create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, the justice secretary told MPs the government's plan to free up capacity in the UK's male prison estate will ensure the justice system "commands the confidence of the British public"

"This is the right thing to do, and I pay tribute to his wife Lissie and mother Debbie (Adlam), who campaigned for this," he said.

"We would like to have gone further, but due to the lack of investment in the previous government's 14 years, we are unable to do so."

He added Labour has been forced to take "tough decisions" because it had inherited a justice system "on the brink of failure".

Norris also told MPs the government plans to "bring forward legislation" to end Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences "once and for all – by the end of this Parliament".

IPPS sentences were used where prisoners were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released if the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy called plans to end IPP sentences a "fag packet policy".

He said: "This is the Government's fifth early release policy in just six weeks since the prime minister took office.

"At every stage, we were told ministers had no choice but to include dangerous criminals, because the alternative would be the collapse of the entire system.

"Now the plan is to stop one group of dangerous criminals leaving prison early by letting a different group of dangerous criminals out instead."

Earlier, Norris told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."

Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.

On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.

In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

Beijing-Taipei tensions a feature at meeting in Palau, with Australia and New Zealand saying the forum – not another country – will determine who attends

China ⁠said it had serious concerns ⁠about Taiwan’s presence at ​the annual Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, warning of “consequences” after the democratically ruled island attended the group’s opening ceremony on Monday.

China views Taiwan as its own territory, and China-Taiwan tensions have ⁠featured prominently at the meeting, which is intended to demonstrate regional unity.

“There will always be consequences,” Qian Bo, China’s special envoy for Pacific island affairs, said of Taiwan attending the event. “It’s not a ⁠threat,” he said, without specifying what the consequences would be.

“This is objected to by all, so this should not have happened. We ​think it’s very inappropriate to do so,” he ‌told reporters on Monday after an opening ‌ceremony in Palau, an archipelago of more than 500 islands that has maintained diplomatic ties with Taiwan.

Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said when asked by reporters about the Chinese envoy’s remarks: “The ‌Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country.

“This is primarily a gathering of the Pacific family … and I look forward to the engagement.”

New Zealand’s foreign minister, Winston Peters, echoed that sentiment, saying the group did not take instructions from countries outside it.

Taiwan’s foreign minister, Lin Chia-lung, said on Monday: “Taiwan is honoured to serve as a partner in the Pacific, continuing to stand with everyone and work together to make the Pacific ‌more prosperous and peaceful.”

Lin Chia-lung was invited for meetings and side events held alongside the forum. Taiwan is not a formal dialogue partner of the forum like ​China, but a development partner. The US, EU, Britain, Canada, India and Japan are also among the 21 dialogue partners of the forum.

China has gradually whittled away the number of Pacific Island countries with formal ties to Taipei, with only three remaining: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands.

The leaders of Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa, Solomon Islands and Kiribati did not attend the gathering of the 18-member group that ⁠counts Australia, New Zealand and Pacific island nations as members. Ministers are attending in their ​place.

China is Australia’s largest trading ​partner but Canberra remains wary of Beijing’s expanding influence ​in the Pacific and has stepped up security and development ties with island nations to deter any ​permanent Chinese military presence in ‌the region.

Australia, New Zealand ​and the US have ​long considered the South Pacific to fall within their sphere of influence. In the latest sign of that effort, New Zealand and the US said in a joint statement released on Tuesday during the summit that they would jointly fund a major upgrade of a second world war port on a Cook Islands atoll.

stories.title: Fatal crash police get £2m to tackle serious crime
stories.summary: The home secretary says the money will help support the force in the aftermath of the A66 crash.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough

Published 1 September 2026

A police force is being given an extra £2m after a spate of crimes followed the death of two police officers and five men in a head-on crash, the home secretary has announced.

Shabana Mahmood pledged the funding after Prime Minister Andy Burnham paid tribute to the officers killed, and in light of the challenges faced by Cleveland Police following the seven deaths on the A66 near Middlesbrough on 22 August.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died when a Volkswagen Passat going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank hit their vehicle. The five men in the Volkswagen also died.

The force has since arrested 27 people for activities linked to "serious and organised crime".

About 200 police officers from outside Cleveland Police have been drafted in to help the force tackle organised crime following the crash.

In the days following the deaths, police dealt with a series of incidents including homes being rammed and vehicles set on fire at a vigil.

Mahmood said "lawlessness of any kind" would "never be tolerated".

"In light of the situation the force has faced, we will allocate an additional £2m to Cleveland Police to tackle serious crime in the area," she said.

She paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash and said she recognised how "unnerving" the current climate would be for the "law abiding citizens" in the community.

She said: "We will do our best to support the Middlesbrough community, which is hurting and grieving right now, and we hear the call from the members of this house representing it for a discussion about investment in policing and police numbers."

'Not a solution'

Conservative MP Chris Philp told Mahmood the extra £2m pledged was "wholly inadequate" and said he was concerned about a shortfall in funding for the force in general.

He said: "This lawless gang chaos should never have been allowed to take root in the first place."

Commenting following the announcement, Cleveland's Labour Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) Matt Storey said a "one-off payment" was "not a solution".

He said: "It does nothing to address the chronic underfunding that has disadvantaged policing in Cleveland for years."

He called on the government to act to address "deep-rooted funding inequalities".

"Cleveland Police needs at least an additional £20m every year to recruit and retain 200 more police officers, to strengthen efforts to crack down on serious and organised crime."

Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said she was committed to reviewing the funding formula, which is used to determine the funding that each force is given.

She added the previous government had taken away 20,000 police officers from forces nationally.

Seven people, including two police officers, died in the wrong-way crash on the A66 on 22 August

The Labour MP for Middlesbrough and Thornaby East, Andy McDonald, told Mahmood that Cleveland Police had the highest rate of crime for any police force in England and Wales.

He said the latest figures showed about 123 recorded crimes per 1,000 residents, yet the force had received the "largest percentage reduction" in officers since 2010.

"Police numbers are not the only factor, but a force facing the highest demand in the country needs the resources to respond," he said.

He added the £2m would address some of the extra funding needed but he wanted to discuss how funding shortfalls could "urgently and permanently be corrected".

Mahmood said she would be happy to meet with MPs in the area to discuss the issue and wider funding concerns.

Luke Myer, Labour MP for Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland, also called for the government to review how funding was assigned.

Mahmood said "reviewing and reforming" the formula was "absolutely critical" and said she would be updating MPs on a schedule for changes to be discussed, once an independent review on police force structures had been completed.

Hong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UK

Shares in the fast-fashion brand Shein slumped by as much as 10% as the China-founded company made its long-anticipated trading debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

The Singapore-headquartered company, once valued at almost $100bn (£74bn), went public on Tuesday pricing shares at HK$48.56, valuing the business at just over $26bn.

However, minutes after the flotation, which raised HK$13.6bn, the stock fell as much as 10%, pushing the online retailer’s valuation below $25bn.

Shein’s share price recovered most of its early trading plunge, closing at HK$48.50, just 0.12% down on its opening price.

“Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion,” said Leigh Gui, Shein’s chief financial officer, after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading.

The lacklustre launch as a publicly listed company comes after one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings in recent years, after plans to list in New York were blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns.

Shein also considered a £50bn flotation in London but faced similar questions about its supply chain from campaigners, MPs and investors.

Nevertheless, the company has still floated as one of the world’s biggest listed fashion groups, with a valuation around the same as the Swedish retailer H&M. The Zara owner, Inditex, has a market capitalisation of about $213bn.

Shein reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world at the time. The plunge in its value since has been driven by regulatory changes around the world that threaten its business model of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods.

The company swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the US removed its “de minimis” import duty exemption on small packages, hitting its sales in the country.

The EU is also cracking down on the loophole, introducing a €3 (£2.56) duty on small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc in June, and intends to phase it out, while the UK has said it will do the same by October 2028.

On Tuesday, France began imposing penalties on some fast-fashion items to curb the surge in sales of cheap products sold by retailers such as Shein and its Chinese rival Temu.

after newsletter promotion

Paris passed a fast-fashion law in June to address concerns about overproduction, with the penalties calculated using a formula that factors in the number of products sold, their prices and repairability.

The penalties, which are set to increase in 2030, range from €0.25 for a pair of boxer shorts or socks to €12 for a coat, with the amount capped at 50% of the product’s pre-tax sales price.

China’s commerce ministry has called the French law discriminatory and a trade barrier and said it could be in violation of World Trade Organization principles.

Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu , runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at about the start of 2022, a move viewed by analysts as designed to avoid increasing scrutiny of Chinese companies.

After forced labour concerns were raised , Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.

stories.body:
While many young people have found jobs and built careers, some have struggled to complete their courses

T he crisis in the youth employment market, with almost a million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the UK, has placed fresh emphasis on ways of getting employees into the workforce.

The government hopes to increase focus on technical and vocational learning in England from the age of 14. In parallel, there is an ambition to create thousands more apprenticeships.

The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has also announced a new bursary aimed at ensuring families will not be left financially worse off if their teenager starts an apprenticeship.

Research from the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) found that black and mixed-ethnicity learners from poorer backgrounds and those for whom English is an additional language are less likely to complete their apprenticeships.

The Guardian asked people to share their experiences of apprenticeships.

‘I am progressing faster than colleagues with degrees’

Ellen*, 24, from Worcester, decided an apprenticeship would work better for her than university, although it was “never suggested” as an option at school.

“It was just assumed that uni was going to be the way I went,” she says. “I did my own research on my other options.”

Securing an apprenticeship was not easy, and she experienced “a lot of rejections” before she won a place at a medium-sized MEP (mechanical, electrical and plumbing) consultancy.

Her three-year apprenticeship was four days a week with a day at college for her higher national certificate (HNC) studies. Her HNC course was two years, but the apprenticeship requirement of submitting evidence added an additional year.

Ellen passed, gaining a BTec level 4 HNC as well as a CIBSE (Chartered Institute of Building Services Engineers) Licentiate, and EngTech certification through CIBSE as an end-point assessment organisation and the UK regulatory body, the Engineering Council.

“It was a huge learning curve and I had to ask for extra help from my teachers,” she says. “At 18, being thrown into the deep end, you just want to do well, you just want to try your best to get all the answers right.

“I had a really good experience at the company that took me on as an apprentice and then gave me a job – really supportive managers – but I found it difficult to balance work, study and having a social life. All my friends chose to go to university and were all over the country, and there was no one around my age at work so having any social life was very difficult.”

Ellen says a “lack of female role models” within her industry and office was also “a difficulty”.

“I have since moved into fire sprinkler design, but starting my new career with a construction qualification and four years of industry experience has meant I am progressing faster than my colleagues who have degrees,” she says.

‘I was effectively being paid to learn’

Harry, 26, a machinist, says he feels “gratitude” that he has a job, as he sees friends who went to university now questioning that decision.

“Some have needed uni to get the jobs that they have now, but some of them I don’t think have needed it, and they’re starting to realise that,” he says.

Harry, from Billingshurst, West Sussex, says that, after achieving three A-levels, he briefly flirted with the idea of studying business at university.

“The cost put me off,” he says. “Also, it didn’t sit right with me in my gut to go to university. I just didn’t think I had the mental strength for full-time education while balancing a part-time job and watching my money.”

Instead, he worked two ski seasons as a chaperone in France and was planning a third when the Covid pandemic closed down tourism.

“I was lucky and privileged enough to be able to come back home to stay with my family,” he says. “They obviously wanted me to get a job to pay rent.”

Harry knew about apprenticeships through his father, who had done an electrician’s apprenticeship in the late 1980s, and applied for “about five”. He got a four-year level 3 engineering machine technician work placement, involving a day a week of study. He started his apprenticeship in 2020, but delays due to Covid meant he finished it in 2025.

Harry threw himself into his studies. “While I was at college, I made sure that all the time I was there, I was doing as much work as I could because I was effectively being paid to learn,” he says.

At the end of his apprenticeship, he gained an engineering technician (machinist – advanced manufacturing engineering) level 3 qualification. The apprenticeship had a guaranteed job if he passed. Harry was offered a role, but he decided to go elsewhere for a better wage.

He adds: “I do take gratitude in the fact that I have a job. People are meant to come out of uni and find a career, but I don’t think many of them can.”

‘Some people were not ready to come to work’

Hannah*, a metalworker, says while her apprenticeship was “amazing”, she saw how others struggled and missed out on completing theirs because of a lack of support.

“The work suited me, and I received plenty of affirmation after a long spell of unemployment and low self-confidence,” she says. “The college qualification opened a lot of doors.

“I took maths and English functional skills tests as part of the process, having not taken any exams as a school-refusing teenager, but the course had some shortcomings when it came to material and delivery – my cohort on the course were almost universally disengaged.”

Hannah, who is in her 30s and lives in south-west England, dropped out of school aged 14, only returning sporadically. She was “in that category of Neet for quite a while”, turning to the apprenticeship after periods in college, cleaning part-time and picking up “little bits of work” in her 20s.

While she is encouraged by the government’s plans regarding technical learning and apprenticeships, she sounds a note of caution. Hannah saw several people unable to continue with their apprenticeship and believes more guided support would have helped, adding that some of the cohort “struggled with attendance and emotional regulation”.

“I think apprenticeships can be fantastic, but they aren’t the panacea for joblessness,” she says. “There’s a lot of really good intentions to try and use the apprenticeship programme to get people who might have been a bit like me, though I was also very privileged because I had a supportive family and wasn’t from a really deprived background.

“But I saw some people on the apprenticeship, particularly the younger ones, who were just not ready to come into work. Some of them had quite complex emotional problems or difficult backgrounds as well, which makes it even harder.”

‘Not having any debt is very freeing’

Jotham, 24, from Buckinghamshire, says he regarded his three-year degree apprenticeship as the “safest route” to securing a job.

“I knew before I did my A-levels that I wanted to do an apprenticeship,” he says. “My dad had said it was a good option and I looked at the government list. University was a backup option if it hadn’t worked out.”

He applied for “about 20 to 30 apprenticeships” and chose a scheme with one day a week studying at university in London that meant he could live at home and commute. It started in 2019.

“The company I chose had two apprentices at the same time, so that was an advantage, as you had someone to do it with, and the previous apprentice was also there and would help us,” he says.

He achieved a first in his digital and technology solutions apprenticeship BSc. Although there was no guarantee of a job at the end of his course, Jotham “carried on working at the same place and was offered a job”.

“It’s a very practical option, isn’t it?” he says. “It has all of the advantages of university and none of the disadvantages. Not having any debt is very freeing.”

However, he knew of some apprentices who were not so lucky: one had to stop “a year in” because the firm collapsed.

“Others either had to stop completely or change how they did the course because the company wasn’t able to employ them for the whole three years,” he adds. “That was a lot of bother for them, because there was no backup plan built into the course.”

Jotham is now working in database management.

“In the job market, really what’s wanted is experience, but people coming out of their degree may struggle to get that,” he says. “With an apprenticeship, you get the experience. The degree is almost like a checkbox item.”

stories.title: Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
stories.summary: The prime minister's first appearance in Parliament comes more than six weeks after he entered No 10.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 September 2026

Andy Burnham has taken questions from MPs in the House of Commons for the first time since taking over as prime minister.

The statement on his future plans for power comes six weeks after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, just before Parliament's summer recess.

Here are the main points from what he said.

He plans to give away power

Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects.

But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not.

He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy.

Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties.

Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there.

He was pressed on defence spending

The statement was the first chance for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to grill Burnham on defence spending following headlines on the issue over the summer.

Chancellor John Healey was appointed by Burnham after quitting as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer , calling for the UK to spend 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2030.

However, since entering the Treasury, Healey is yet to attach a date to this spending target, and has faced pressure to do so in recent days.

Healey has said a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP will be set out at the next government spending review, expected in spring next year.

But in a potential signal of his intentions in this area, Burham said the arguments Healey had made about defence spending in his former role were a key reason why he had put him in charge of the Treasury.

Andy Burnham chaired his first Number 10 North meeting in July

He will go to the UN's climate summit

Burnham confirmed he would attend the COP31 climate summit in November, as he vowed to "meet the climate challenge".

The annual UN climate change conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, allowing Burnham to come face to face with many world leaders and senior officials.

While Sir Keir attended COP summits when he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak was criticised in 2022 for not going because he had "other pressing domestic commitments".

Burnham's pledge to attend the summit comes as he faces a looming decision about whether to allow drilling to start in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, in the North Sea, which have been in legal limbo for a year.

He wants to continue leasehold reform

Labour's 2024 election manifesto promised to "finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end", after campaigners said it was unfair that flat owners had little control over spiralling property costs.

A draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill published by Starmer's government earlier this year included plans to cap ground rent at £250, ban the sale of new leasehold flats and give homeowners greater control over how their buildings are managed.

Under the bill, leasehold would be banned "except in limited cases", and developers would no longer be allowed to sell new flats as leasehold.

That bill is yet to be introduced to Parliament, but Burnham confirmed he intended to "bring forward" a Commonhold and Leasehold Bill during the current session of Parliament, which began in May and would normally last around a year.

He paid tribute to Starmer

Burnham kicked off his Commons statement by paying tribute to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who had announced he was resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras just hours earlier.

Sir Keir had given the UK "a lifetime of service", Burnham said, including delivering the Hillsborough Law which demands more accountability from public officials during official inquiries, as well as work to achieve peace in Ukraine.

He also praised Sir Keir for leading Labour to one of its "best victories" in the 2024 election.

He said Sir Keir had "created a platform to change this country for the better" which the new government would "use well".

A graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’

D rinking Tsingtao beers, eating congee, walking with hands behind their backs: for many young people in western countries, “ Chinamaxxing ” has become all the rage. Some content creators have even gone beyond the jokes about being in “a very Chinese time in my life” and have followed this passion to the Middle Kingdom: making TikToks in Chongqing’s multilayered metropolis, bathing in Chengdu’s 24-hour spas or backflipping on the Great Wall of China.

This irreverent, mostly ironic trend is jarring for some, but Chinese Australian artist Badiucao and Chinese American journalist Melissa Chan don’t want to lecture the so-called Chinamaxxers.

“The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society. They feel defeated when they see what’s happening in Gaza – there’s been protests but the government doesn’t care and is collaborating with atrocities in wars. There’s also the Epstein files in America, which show how the elite is corrupt,” says Badiucao, who, along with Chan, is in Sydney to promote their new book, You Must Take Part in Revolution.

“When you want to see change, there is the hard way, which is being innovative and finding a solution. And there is the lazy way, which is finding a cheap alternative and fantasising about a faraway, oriental, communist country that might be your future,” he says.

Chan and Badiucao have both paid the price for criticising China’s one-party system. Chinese officials refused to renew Chan’s press credentials before expelling the former Al Jazeera journalist from China in 2012; and the previously anonymous political cartoonist Badiucao was forced to reveal his identity in 2019 after it was compromised and authorities threatened his family in China.

You Must Take Part in Revolution, the pair’s debut graphic novel, portrays a dystopian future where China is at war with the United States in 2035.

The graphic novel features a variety of characters from the Chinese-speaking diaspora, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the US and Tibet, as they decide what choices they are willing to make under authoritarian oppression.

“It was intentional to show the panoply of Asian identities that have been impacted by a great power,” Chan says. “It opens up the possibility to get young people to better understand it’s not just a ‘Chinese time in my life’, that there’s a lot going on here … hopefully it can get a few people thinking about resistance movements both present and in the past.”

“We don’t want to just lecture,” Badiucao adds. “We really want readers to put themselves in the eyes of those characters as if they were a real human being with a real life.”

Chan now lives in Berlin and has written for the Atlantic, the Washington Post, Time, and others, while Badiucao, who lives in Melbourne, has exhibited works across the world. They started working on the graphic novel five years ago after first meeting in Germany during the late 2010s.

You Must Take Part in Revolution starts off in the real-life Hong Kong protests of 2019, when almost two million people took to the streets to denounce a controversial law that would allow the extradition of suspects to mainland China. The law was viewed as a sign of growing mainland influence in Hong Kong.

While the graphic novel is geographically grounded in an Asia governed by authoritarian China, it also portrays the US as a proto-fascist state, resisting the idea that criticising one necessarily means painting the other in a positive light.

“This book happens to focus on China, but authoritarianism everywhere is bad,” Chan says. “We don’t want anyone to engage in whataboutism and I don’t think there needs to be a balance – if things are shit, they’re shit in any country.”

Unlike other graphic novels such as Art Spiegelman’s Maus, Badiucao and Chan’s book takes its influence from Japanese manga. “There are great works like Attack on Titan which are not necessarily about specific history or political content that have so many metaphors reflecting important things like racism, war and equity,” Badiucao says.

“It’s part of the reason this form is potentially more than just entertainment or some kid stuff, it really influences an entire generation.”

You Must Take Part in Revolution was released in the US in 2025, but it is only just getting its Australian release this week and its UK release in October.

Badiucao says readers across the world have contacted them about their own histories after reading it, including Ukrainian refugees who have escaped Russia’s invasion, and Czech communities who lived through the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.

The artist recalls one interaction at a comic festival in New York, where a second-generation Chinese Canadian girl told him that she had hesitations about taking the book home. “I don’t think my mum would love it,” she said.

A few minutes later, an older woman came up to Badiucao and explained she was an immigrant whose family had been through hardship during the Cultural Revolution. Flipping through the book, she said her daughter might like it, but she didn’t know if she would be open to learning about Chinese politics.

Badiucao later discovered the two were mother and daughter.

“I told the daughter her mum might be more open about political stuff, and I told the mum that your daughter might be interested too,” he says. “They ended up having an honest conversation, and they got a copy of the book … among all the interactions with readers, that was pretty special to me.”

You Must Take Part in Revolution by Melissa Chan and Badiucao is out now in Australia (Affirm Press; $39.99), as well as in the US. It is out in the UK on 8 October.
