stories.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
stories.summary: The move will trigger a by-election to replace the former prime minister in his London constituency.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Since he resigned as prime minister in July, there was speculation over whether Sir Keir would stay on as MP

Published 1 September 2026

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament .

"He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added.

"His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."

Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal , external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

'Another U-turn'

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wished Sir Keir the best for the future adding: "I can understand why he would not want to spend time with the Labour MPs who treated him so badly after he won them their seats."

Tory Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Sir Keir of making "another U-turn having pledged to stay on", prompting a "costly by-election for taxpayers".

A date will not be set for the by-election until Sir Keir formally resigns his Commons seat.

This will only be confirmed once the government has given him a crown appointment, the mechanism that disqualifies him from being an MP.

Labour expects to select a candidate for the by-election by 9 September, according to the party's website.

Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, with Sir Keir securing a more than 11,000-vote majority at the last general election in 2024.

Labour's main challenger in the seat is likely to be the Greens, who came second by vote totals at this year's local elections in wards that make up the constituency - with 29.8% of the vote to Labour's 39.5%.

Reform UK came a distant third by these vote totals, and the Greens' share was higher if they are given the votes in two wards where they stood aside.

Candidates for the by-election will not be confirmed until a later stage, but the Greens hinted that leader Zack Polanski was considering a run at the seat.

A spokesperson for the party said Polanski, currently a member of the London Assembly, had "always made it clear he would like to be a London MP".

Starmer: What Went Wrong?

From triumph to turmoil, the story of how Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership unravelled, from Labour’s historic 2024 landslide to the fatal miscalculations and internal revolt that forced him from power.

Previous PMs

While it is unclear exactly what type of international affairs role Sir Keir may take up, global issues and diplomacy dominated his time as PM.

In his departure interview in July, Sir Keir was asked if he had another big political or international job in him, to which he replied: "I don't know is the honest answer to that."

By standing down so soon after quitting as PM , Sir Keir has departed from recent precedent for those in Downing Street before him.

Rishi Sunak is still the Tory MP for Richmond and Northallerton two years after leaving No 10, and his precedessor Liz Truss stayed on as a backbencher until she lost her seat to Labour at the 2024 election.

Theresa May stayed on as MP for five years after leaving Downing Street.

However, both Boris Johnson and David Cameron quit the Commons shortly afterwards.

stories.title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
stories.summary: The UK says Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 September 2026

Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.

The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported , external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

Trump's remarks were labelled "nonsense" by Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, as she asked the UK government to issue an official response in the House of Commons.

Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran replied: "The UK has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

"They are and will always remain a British overseas territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders.

"The UK is steadfast in our support for the islanders' rights of self-determination."

Kumaran said she had seen Trump's comments, adding: "Our position remains unchanged."

Defence spending pledges

In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.

The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

Reports of this proposal have re-emerged in recent days in relation to defence spending.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will honour a commitment made by predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to devote 3.5% of UK gross domestic product (GDP) on core defence spending by 2035.

On Tuesday, Chancellor John Healey told The Times , external he would "set out a clear path" to meeting that Nato pledge at the next government spending review, expected in the spring of next year.

He added that this would also include a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP.

Healey resigned as defence secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government following a row over military spending.

His resignation letter in June expressed his frustration that the government had no clear timetable to hit the 3% spending target, which he believed should happen by 2030.

Chagos deal questions

The UK government has also faced questions over whether it will continue with a deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.

It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.

Kumaran told MPs on Tuesday that "maintaining long-term operational control and security of the base remains a top priority and is the entire basis for the UK-Mauritius agreement."

The minister also said funding for the treaty would be provided for "within the existing spending review settlements" for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the Ministry of Defence.

Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge criticised the remarks and said the deal "belongs on the ash heap of history".

He said in a statement: "Burnham should show some backbone and break with this terrible legacy of the Starmer years by ditching his crazy Chagos deal once and for all, and spending the savings on our armed forces."

In the Commons, Conservative shadow Foreign Office minister Wendy Morton noted Sir Keir's administration acknowledged in April that the Chagos treaty had become "impossible to agree at political level" and asked what had changed.

Kumaran said the Burnham government would "continue to work with the US and Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK's best interests and protects our national security".

stories.title: New laws planned to tackle rogue funeral firms
stories.summary: The government plans to regulate undertakers after the jailing of Hull funeral director Robert Bush.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The law change comes after police investigated Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull

Published 1 September 2026

A minister has said the government is working on new laws to "drive rogue operators out of the funeral industry".

Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Yvette Cooper gave a written update to Parliament on proposed legislation to regulate undertakers.

It comes after a Hull funeral home director was jailed last month for failing to bury or cremate people and giving bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers.

Robert Bush was sent to prison for 20 years after he admitted 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial, theft from charities, and fraudulent trading over a period of almost 12 years.

During his sentencing, Hull Crown Court heard that 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found by police raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in March 2024.

Bush, 48, of Otley in West Yorkshire, was "preoccupied with his own enrichment", defrauded nearly 200 families out of £562,117 and "caused anguish and pain on a scale beyond comprehension", the judge said.

Cooper said Bush's actions were "utterly abhorrent, and my thoughts remain with all the bereaved families in Hull who were so badly let down."

She said that, as part of the plans, the Law Commission would review the criminal law in relation to the deceased and "consider any gaps in existing legal protections and make recommendations on the creation of new offences, if they are needed".

Cooper said detailed plans and the timetable for their introduction would be announced "in due course".

Robert Bush was jailed at Hull Crown Court for 20 years last month

The funeral industry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is currently self-regulating, relying on voluntary codes and inspections by trade associations.

Anyone can set up as a funeral director without formal training, registration or oversight.

MPs and families affected by Bush's crimes have been lobbying for change.

Nigel Hotham's uncle, Mark Hotham, died in September 2023 and his body was later found in Bush's funeral parlour.

"It's easier to open a funeral director's than it is to open a sandwich shop – and there's more regulation around sandwich shops than there is funeral directors," he said.

Reform UK's Richard Tice questioned on BBC local radio

Published 1 September 2026

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice has defended decisions to raise council tax and cut spending at local authorities led by the party in England.

Tice faced questions about the party's record in local government in a round of interviews with BBC radio stations ahead of its annual conference this week.

He was asked why Reform UK-led councils had raised council tax, with presenters suggesting the party had given the impression it would do the opposite.

Tice argued Reform UK councillors had shown they were "financially prudent" and were "doing a good job of getting to grips with wasteful spending".

The BBC interviews focused on Reform UK's policies in local government, where the party gained control of 24 councils following local elections this May and last year.

But they also covered national issues and the role of Nigel Farage, following a difficult summer of questions about a £5m gift received and not declared by Reform UK's leader.

The gift, and the parliamentary investigation into it, attracted more attention than the party would have liked in recent months, distracting from its policy announcements on immigration and welfare.

Asked whether he would be prepared to lead the party, should Farage stand down, Tice insisted "Nigel is going nowhere" and would lead the party into the next general election.

The party's conference in Birmingham this week is an opportunity for Reform UK to regain some political initiative and show it is capable of governing.

The party's conference, Tice said, would be about "the first 100 days of a Reform government".

He said Reform UK would be talking about "hope, optimism, and how to create some growth as we start to rebuild Britain".

Council tax came up several times in the interviews with Tice.

In March this year, Farage pledged that if his party took control of further councils in May's local elections, it would ensure council tax rises in those areas would be lower than in those run by any of the other parties.

Tice said a council tax rise of 9% in Worcestershire , while Reform UK was in minority control of the county council, was the "right and proper thing".

Speaking to BBC Hereford & Worcester, he said: "We had to be honest with people and say the council is effectively bust."

Reform UK lost control of the county council on 14 May, after councillors from the party ousted their own leader before a coalition made up of the Green Party, Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and independents took over.

Other topics in the interviews included spending cuts by Durham County Council , led by Reform UK.

Tice said he "trusted our councillors to make those judgements themselves".

He told BBC Radio Cornwall that more affordable housing was "absolutely vital" in areas like theirs, adding his party would introduce a right-to-buy scheme to help people get on the ladder.

He told BBC Radio Leicester climate change was real, but the government should focus on adapting to it - rather than "arrogantly thinking we can stop it".

BBC Radio Newcastle asked Tice if Reform UK was doing enough to ensure professional standards in local government after resignations, expulsions and suspensions in the north east of England, and he responded that "the most professional thing to do is save money".

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent, Tice said Reform UK was "driving the way the decisions are being made" on the Isle of Wight after winning 19 of 39 seats in May.

UK borrowing costs driven up, adding to challenges facing John Healey as he prepares for first budget

Business live – latest updates

The global government bond sell-off resumed on Wednesday, driving up the UK’s borrowing costs and exacerbating the challenges facing John Healey as he prepares his first budget.

The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, or gilts, jumped to just below 5.3% in early trading: its highest level since mid-2008.

Investors across major markets have been dumping bonds in recent days amid fears about inflation and spiralling deficits.

Global inflation fears have intensified since the US and Iran began exchanging fire again at the weekend, pushing up the oil price and increasing expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates in the coming months.

Higher bond yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. UK analysts have warned that higher gilt yields since the start of the Iran war have potentially wiped out almost half of Healey’s headroom against the government’s fiscal rules.

Economists at Deutsche Bank reckon the £26bn room for manoeuvre Rachel Reeves created at her spring forecast could be down to less than £14bn by the time of the 28 October budget.

Healey would then have to decide whether to rebuild the margin for error with tax increases or spending cuts – alongside facing pressure to fund higher defence spending.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, said: “Governments around the world are feeling the pressure from bond markets, but the situation is particularly acute for the UK, where Andy Burnham’s grand promises about reforming the economy are about to meet the cold reality of high debt levels and rocketing borrowing costs.”

after newsletter promotion

The Brent crude oil benchmark is currently hovering at about $95 a barrel amid renewed fighting in the Middle East. The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets overnight , prompting counterstrikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Gulf allies.

The resumption of the sell-off in UK markets came after Asian stock markets fell sharply. In Tokyo the Nikkei 225 share index slumped by 2.85%. China’s CSI 300 lost 1.4%, while South Korea’s Kospi dropped by 3.3%.

Investors have also been rattled in recent days by the US administration’s attempts to interfere in financial markets – including helping the Japanese to prop up the value of the yen and buying back more US government bonds, or treasuries, to rein in rising yields. Neither move appears to have been successful.

stories.body:
Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods

Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods , ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said.

The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border.

About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water.

As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall.

Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.

The swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.

Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region.

Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.

About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.

The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.

Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”

His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.

The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”

Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.

“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”

The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”

The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions .

Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.

“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.

Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.

“There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”

Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.

Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response.

Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse.

China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.

Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.

Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.

The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.

In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been ​homes , trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.

China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.

stories.title: Burghart becomes Tory deputy leader in major reshuffle
stories.summary: The move completes a shake-up of Kemi Badenoch's top team ahead of the party's conference in October.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alex Burghart is expected to stand in for Kemi Badenoch when she is not present for PMQs

Published 31 August 2026

Alex Burghart has been appointed deputy leader of the Conservative Party, as part of a major reshuffle that saw Sir Mel Stride and Dame Priti Patel sacked.

Burghart has been a close ally of Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, often helping her prepare for Prime Minister's Question Time and big Commons moments.

His appointment is the final element of Badenoch's substantial shadow cabinet reshuffle, much of which took place on Monday.

In other moves, Andrew Griffith will replace Sir Mel as shadow chancellor, while Tom Tugendhat will take the place of Dame Priti as shadow foreign secretary.

With most polls putting the Conservatives in third place, lagging behind Labour and Reform UK, Badenoch will be hoping a refreshed shadow cabinet will help boost her party's popularity ahead of the party's conference in October.

Burghart is expected to be the go-to stand-in at PMQs, and also deputise for Badenoch when necessary, as well as continuing as Shadow Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and Shadow Northern Ireland Secretary.

He was elected as MP for Brentwood and Ongar in Essex on the same day Badenoch was elected in the nearby constituency now known as North West Essex in 2017.

A senior Conservative source said: "Kemi is changing the way the Conservative Party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility."

Badenoch said that as shadow chancellor, Sir Mel had helped the party rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition.

Sir Mel, who was appointed to the role following Badenoch's leadership election in 2024, described his time in post as a "great honour".

New shadow chancellor Griffith said the Tories will deliver "an economic revolution" with lower taxes, Britain drilling again to bring energy costs down, slashing red tape and Labour's Employment Rights Act.

"The Conservatives will always back the risk-takers and wealth creators who deliver growth, investment and jobs," he said.

The Tory source described Griffith as a "no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience".

Claire Coutinho, previously the shadow energy secretary, after her maternity leave will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary and act as his deputy.

Opposition parties highlight Andrew Griffith's role in the 2022 Liz Truss mini-Budget

Before he became MP for Arundel and South Downs in 2019, Griffith served as a top executive at Sky and as chairman of Just Eat.

As a Treasury minister, he defended Liz Truss' 2022 mini-Budget .

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson described Griffith as "a key architect of Liz Truss's disastrous mini-Budget" and said the shadow cabinet featured politicians "who hammered family finances and left our public services crumbling".

That message was echoed by other parties. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "His appointment to shadow chancellor shows they're happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility in their race to the bottom with Reform UK."

Reform UK's economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "They haven't changed and still aren't sorry for the damage they inflicted on our country."

Dame Priti, who had been shadow foreign secretary since 2024, will return to the backbenches and will take on a new international role strengthening the Tories relationship with sister parties and centre-right movements abroad.

Badenoch has selected Damian Hinds as the new shadow health and social care secretary after Stuart Andrew confirmed he will be returning to the backbenches .

Katie Lam has been named as the new housing secretary, after Sir James Cleverly quit the front bench, announcing he wants to run for London mayor .

Claire Coutinho will become shadow business secretary after maternity leave

Badenoch's reshuffle is intended to bring solutions to a number of problems.

First, she wants to retire those members of her top team that have had a relatively low profile, or who have not been delivering sufficient blows to both Labour and Reform UK.

Badenoch paid a warm tribute to Sir Mel but some recent polls suggested that Reform UK were more trusted on the economy than the Conservatives.

And that is something Kemi Badenoch felt needed to change.

Second, while familiar faces like Dame Priti were useful to have in the top team as they brought high-level government experience, they might also remind voters of the party they decisively rejected in 2024.

There has been a changing of the old guard, and Badenoch is now focusing on who can take the Conservatives into the next election - faced as she is by a new Labour leader and cabinet.

Third, she wants to focus on issues where Labour is perceived to be vulnerable.

One such area is defence spending and national security.

So as shadow foreign secretary she appointed Tom Tugendhat - a former security minister and current army reservist who served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He will work as part of a team with the shadow defence secretary.

Some opinion polls rate the economy as the most important issue for voters, above asylum and immigration, and again the Tory leader believes the government is vulnerable here, with sluggish growth.

So she has announced a new Conservative economic unit headed by Griffith, with his extensive business experience.

Coutinho as his deputy is seen as a rising Conservative star who has performed well in her previous role shadowing the former energy secretary Ed Miliband in the Commons, and as a potential future chancellor if the Conservatives were ever to recover electorally.

But the Tory leader has also included the former Conservative chairman and City Minister Richard Fuller in the unit, concentrating on fiscal responsibility and tax.

He will be deployed as an attack dog if - as she believes he will – the chancellor raises taxes in the Budget.

But the role will also underline that the Conservative leader is serious about making her sums add up, in contrast to her characterisation of Reform UK's plans as ill-thought out.

The question now though is whether Badenoch will change her own approach to political leadership.

While some of her top team may be seen as lacklustre, how much opportunity did they get to shine?

She tends to make the big announcements and is ubiquitous on the media.

If the Conservatives are to convince voters they are once again a government in waiting then the public will have to see that there is breadth and depth in the team that is shadowing current ministers.

stories.body:
US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles

Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia.

But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined.

An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US.

Among the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec.

Canadian provisions include legislation that mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”.

For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,” he told CNBC , dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”.

“My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.”

The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen by some Canadian officials as a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue.

“President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” he told CBC , the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.”

The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed a retributive executive order supposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade.

And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control.

Moving the goalposts

Those who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise.

“I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.”

It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand.

According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act .

Carney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical.

“Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was.

“From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.”

Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage.

“I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

after newsletter promotion

‘Trump whisperer’

Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020.

He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress.

“He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.”

Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing.

He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence.

Navarro, who went to jail for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week.

Asked to respond to an article in the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us.

“Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.”

Blame game

Navarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US.

“Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.”

Yet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out.

“The larger Canadian objection was not due to interagency American disagreement,” Reinsch said. “Trump has very strong fixed views on trade. He thinks tariffs are good. So if you’re going to blame somebody, don’t blame Lutnick or Greer. Blame Trump, because I’m quite confident he had the last word on this.”

Regardless of where blame is apportioned, the consequences of Carney’s defiance will reverberate beyond Canada, analysts say, as other countries forced to confront Trump’s threats of tariffs reassess and recalibrate how they should respond.

“Other countries are watching the developments with Canada very closely,” said Cutler. “Some of our other trading partners have expressed similar frustrations [to the Canadians] to me privately, and so we could be at a turning point.

“It is possible that what we’re experiencing with Canada now spreads to other countries.”

stories.body:
Rights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admits

A Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the Tibetan side of the border in last week’s deadly floods, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.

Public discussion about the flash floods has been restricted, with security officials in Tibet announcing on Sunday that it had penalised at least 10 people for sharing “false disaster information”. There was no further information on the nature of the penalties.

Chinese authorities say 16 people have been confirmed dead and 546 are missing, including 261 foreign citizens. But the International Campaign for Tibet says its sources believe the number of casualties is significantly higher, with at least 300 homes destroyed.

Tencho Gyatso, the president of the campaign group, told the Guardian: “What is visible in Nepal exposes what is being concealed in Tibet. Four villages – Sale, Serchung, Labi and Rizi – were among the hardest hit, with approximately 300 homes reportedly destroyed and many people still missing.”

She said the “little information that we can gather from the ground” suggested the numbers affected were “far higher” than Chinese officials had reported.

On 26 August, the collapse of a glacier triggered deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages. The death toll on the Nepal side has passed 900, with more than 4,000 missing. Tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada among others remain unaccounted for in the mountainous region that is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Advocacy groups say there has been a stark contrast in the amount of information presented on either side of the border. Chinese coverage has been dominated by official state media reports , with few unofficial accounts about the scale of the disaster and its aftermath.

Independent verification is extremely difficult in Tibet, where foreign journalists face severe restrictions. Tibetans can face imprisonment for sharing information with journalists and advocacy groups outside China .

Gyatso said: “Officially released glimpses, however important, cannot tell us what is happening across all affected communities.”

Her Tibetan advocacy group said several sources reported that survivors had been moved to Gyirong, which is about 30km (18 miles) from the border crossing that was hit by the flooding. They are said to be under strict management and restricted from communicating freely.

According to a report posted on 27 August on the Tibet Daily, a state-run newspaper, two Tibetans were detained for questioning for posting “rumours” that more than 1,000 people had been swept away close to the border.

Gyatso said: “The Chinese government portrays it like it’s only happening in Nepal and there’s nothing across the border. For any type of crisis, the way China handles it is that there is no crisis. The party is in control.”

Posts relating to the disaster continued to trend on Chinese social media on Monday, with many comments echoing official narratives and supporting rescue efforts.

A Weibo post by Hu Xijin – a prominent Chinese commentator and former chief editor of the state-run Global Times – attracted more than 300 comments and thousands of likes. He accused a small number of voices of seeking to “stir controversy by fabricating baseless claims”.

However, one comment under his post questioned why all the updates were coming from the Nepali side of the border.

On Sunday, Tibetan public security officials said they had penalised people for sharing misleading information or “disrupting online order” with posts about the disaster.

In one case, a user identified only as Zhang disputed the official death toll, posting: “Clearly thousands of people were swept away, yet the authorities reported only three deaths and 265 people missing.”

Another user named Zhou said: “In this wave of mudslides, one entire village was wiped out. It was definitely more than a thousand [deaths].”

Maya Wang of Human Rights Watch said: “The instinct of the Chinese government is always to kind of control and to ensure the narrative which is to portray itself as a very efficient government.

“There have been questions raised over how the development of the valleys in an ecologically fragile and geologically fragile area may have related to this disaster.”

Human rights groups say that Beijing maintains tight controls over movement, religion and information in Tibet. Tibetan groups in exile have long been critical of large-scale development in the region, which they consider geologically fragile.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said ⁠on Monday that the ⁠release of ⁠information about the floods and mudslide near its ⁠border with Nepal was transparent and timely.

“Malicious smear campaigns ‌and hype using the disaster situation does not align with popular sentiment,” said Guo Jiakun, ‌in response to allegations that China censored videos of the disaster and understated the number of missing people.

When asked about allegations ‌that China ignored warnings from scientists over hydropower construction, he said: “We ⁠firmly oppose such baseless and malicious speculation.”

stories.body:
Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars

For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.

Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves.

Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%.

The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos.

In truth, long before Donald Trump’s latest sanctions push , Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control.

On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record.

Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%.

As purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods.

Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market.

According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages.

Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.”

Mohsen Zavaar, a biomedical engineer, said: “For part of the population, the issue is no longer buying a house or a car; the issue is cutting out meat, reducing food quality, postponing medical treatment, and scraping by until the end of the month.”

Frustrated by the inability of officials to tackle the problems, he added: “The people don’t want miracles – they want decisions.”

The crisis has spread beyond food and clothes. Long lines of cars stretched through parts of Tehran and the north-eastern Iranian city of Mashhad on Tuesday and Wednesday as motorists queued for fuel, with some lines blocking entire streets. Many petrol stations, including some of the largest, were closed.

Officials blamed isolated panic buying caused by rumours of a government-planned price increase, or Israeli bombs that destroyed two of Tehran’s three main oil depots.

Inside the government, anxious discussions have been under way for weeks about increasing the price of oil to reduce costly subsidies, but the political class know from past experience that there could be significant pushback. A sudden overnight petrol price rise of 50% in November 2019 sparked week-long violent protests .

Public anger has been exacerbated by an admission that vested interests in the government made it hard to tackle fuel smuggling.

Saqab Esfahani, deputy to Iran’s president, said: “Both political factions in the country are involved in fuel smuggling, and if I were to shut down their operations, they would break my windows.”

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been urged to investigate the remarks.

However, transparency over the economic conditions in Iran is likely to decrease.

Fatemeh Mohajerani, a spokesperson for the Iranian government, said recently that future poverty statistics would only be published with the permission of the country’s supreme national security council, making the decline in living standards akin to a classified state secret.

Iran’s leaders now cast the home front as part of the war against America. Hojatoleslam Taeb, the new head of the Basij paramilitary force and a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, recently delivered a speech that conjured up an image of resistance against market forces distorted by US sanctions.

As part of this war, he said it was necessary to reduce petrol consumption by as much as 10% to reduce the need for expensive imports. Avoiding unnecessary travel would be an act of patriotism, he implied.

But these patriotic appeals increasingly have an air of desperation as the economic crisis becomes worse.

Mohsen Rezaei, the new, more hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, said: “I advise young people to start producing the products they and society need in their homes, just as they gather in public spaces.”

Mohammad Taheri, editor of the economics magazine Tejarat Farda, said the advice reminded him of Mao’s “backyard steel furnaces” during the Great Leap Forward. Mao encouraged people to produce their own steel, with disastrous effect.

Amirhossein Hashemi-Javid, an energy expert, said Iran’s true economic crisis was its inability to export oil due to the US blockade. “The channels for selling Iranian oil are drying up.

“Oil that cannot reach customers from the well provides no revenue for the Iranian economy; it is simply barrels that incur increasing production, storage and risk costs every day,” he said.

At some point, the Iranian government will have to decide if it might achieve more through diplomacy than through continued confrontation.

Only six months on from starting a war, after Trump promised protesters in January that help was on its way , the only commodity the US is now offering Iranians is deeper poverty.

stories.title: EFF to Governor Newsom: Veto California’s AB 1709
stories.summary: The California legislature passed Assembly Bill 1709 (A.B. 1709) today, which functions as a sweeping ban on social media use for young people under the age of 16. This well-intentioned, but deeply flawed piece of legislation, cuts young people off from essential information and experiences, particularly harming vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. That’s why we’re urging Governor Gavin Newsom to veto the measure . Should the law go into effect in January, platforms would be prohibited from offering virtually every functional recommendation algorithm and basic input, such as who a user follows or what posts they like, to anyone under 16. These so-called "addictive features," are in reality the basic tools that online services use to identify what other user-generated content a particular user might want to see. Users also rely on these features to find audiences for their own speech, as well as community. By labeling these basic tools as "addictive," the bill relies on sweeping generalizations regarding the unsettled science of youth social media use. Because nearly every major service relies on automated feeds, the ultimate result is that young people under 16 will still be locked out of major digital services as they currently exist. A.B. 1709 is a massive privacy and free speech nightmare. A.B. 1709 is a massive privacy and free speech nightmare. stories.title: EFF to Courts: Don’t Rewrite Copyright Over AI Hype
stories.summary: The history of technology is rife with copyright panics. In the 1980s, major rightsholders ran to Congress and the courts, claiming that videotape recorders (VTR) were “to the American film producer and the American public as the Boston strangler is to the woman home alone .” Then, the Supreme Court declined to embrace the hype, noting that the VTR was capable of all kinds of non-infringing uses, like time-shifting and cautioning courts to avoid rewriting copyright law in response to new technologies. We believe that courts now should be similarly wary about the hype surrounding AI. Hollywood’s hyperbole has echoed that of composer John Phillip Sousa , who claimed in 1906 that the player piano and the gramophone would destroy music composition; portrait artists who feared the camera would replace the paintbrush. None of these things happened. Cameras, for example, sparked a resurgence of portraiture and, by making it possible for more people to create images, led to unexpected developments—like the rise of photojournalism. New markets, new ideas, and new creators are actually what copyright is supposed to promote, not restrict. Using copyright to lock in existing gatekeepers and massive rightsholders’ profits helps neither the public nor individual artists. Generative AI has sparked the latest wave of anxiety and with it a massive wave of litigation. In multiple cases around the U.S. and the world, rightsholders are asking courts to do precisely what the Supreme Court warned against: dramatically expand copyright protections based in substantial part on hyperbole and speculation. They should decline to do so. Copyright owners claim that unless courts abandon 300-year-old copyright principles—and give rightsholders the power to control non-infringing works created by others—an imagined flood of AI-generated works will devastate creative markets. Under this “market dilution” theory, building generative AI tools cannot be fair use because those tools might be encourage the proliferation of competing works. As EFF has explained to the courts in multiple amicus briefs in Concord Music Group, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC and In re Mosaic LLM Litigation , that’s not how copyright works. stories.title: Doxxing Safety Part II: Incident Response
stories.summary: Doxxing, also known as the deliberate sharing of personal information to harass or endanger someone, is a tricky thing to protect against. It often happens by some ill-intentioned person accessing publicly available information, then sharing that information more widely in the hopes it will intimidate their target or worse. This guide is a followup from a previous post that describes a methodology for you to clean up your digital footprint and get a firm entry into the art of open source intelligence. There's a slight bit of repetition here, but with a slant towards using those now-familiar tools and methods toward what to do in the context of incident response. The best thing you can do is familiarize yourself with this post and its tactics before something happens, then return back to it for reference when needed. Incident Log An incident log is a way to keep track of suspicious or harmful activity online. It doesn't need to be beautiful or complex, just a place where you can quickly note details around the different things you're seeing online. Noting times, places, people, and the general nature of what you see ought to be enough. In the event that law enforcement gets involved, this sort of record will be helpful. The process of finding and noting hateful incidents online can be incredibly stressful, so now is a good time to revisit the team roles you might have already thought of in the previous blog post . If you haven't yet done that, here's a brief refresher: Assign Team Roles Remember, privacy–and responding to doxxing–is a team sport. Knowing who you trust is as important as identifying threat actors. Having trusted people ready to assist is invaluable in this type of situation. Refer them to this blog post or specific recommendations in it. If you've already plotted out a list of designated team roles, now is the time to remind everyone of their responsibilities. That might look like monitoring the hate forums where activity happens, keeping track of events in the incident log, setting up web alerts, locking down your social media accounts, or contacting law enforcement to reduce the likelihood of SWATing (a type of attack where bad actors call the police on their target, hoping to incite violence or disruption of peace by bringing law enforcement to their door). stories.title: Doxxing Safety Pt I: Prevention and Footprint Management
stories.summary: Doxxing is the deliberate disclosure of personal information in order to bully, harass, intimidate, or instigate a chain of harms against someone. It's a tricky thing to protect against when the jerk doing it is often able to use legal and accessible means to do so. The odds are stacked against everyday internet folk when there's little to no comprehensive data privacy legislation keeping us safe. The responsibility is on each of us to protect ourselves, but the good news is that there's a lot you can do to reduce your digital footprint and take control of your data. This post is part one of a two-part series discussing safety and response to doxxing. This first part focuses on prevention and ways to reduce your overall footprint. The second focuses on incident response, as in, steps to take if you're in the midst of being doxxed. There will be some crossover and redundancy between these two posts, so it's worth reading each and gaining familiarity with the steps well ahead of time. OSINT Open source intelligence (OSINT) is a broad term within information security. It focuses on the tools and means available to us for investigation and information retrieval. OSINT sits at the heart of doxxing campaigns but is also an important part of the process of preventing them. Typically it is a way of describing a methodology of piecing together scraps of information to form a dossier on a subject. There are fancy multipurpose tools (like Maltego or Lampyre) that combine many datapoints into accessible graphs and datasets. As helpful as they can be for traditional penetration tests or corporate OSINT campaigns, they’re best used for investigations focused on organizations, mapping together details like employee email charts, LinkedIn profiles, and company network maps. They may not fit the needs of everyday people or liberation movement workers. Instead, we recommend referring to different OSINT resource lists that index together a bunch of different tools, then using those resources to create a list for yourself of which tools may be most helpful. Many, if not all, of the resources we cover below will be referenced in those guides, and themselves fall under the OSINT category. stories.title: Privacy on the Map (Part 2): Progress, Pitfalls, and the Fight for Enforceable Location Data Protections
stories.summary: Regulating commercial location tracking has reached a turning point. Last year, we published our rubric for what comprehensive and protective location privacy laws should look like, outlining the baseline standards states should meet to shield individuals from pervasive location surveillance. Since then, state lawmakers across the country have begun responding to calls like these, with Connecticut , Maryland , New Jersey , Oregon , and Virginia enacting new consumer privacy restraints on an industry that profits off our physical movements. Yet, even as these states move the ball forward to restrict location tracking, most of their laws leave significant gaps that still must be filled. Other states – and Congress – need to get into the game, too, and ensure protection of everyone. Why Location Privacy Is Important Imagine spending a couple of hours in a coffee shop, a friend's house, or a healthcare clinic, only to discover yourself under police investigation because your cell phone’s location data exposed your presence there. This is the reality of geofence warrants for location data , the controversial surveillance technique recently scrutinized by the U.S. Supreme Court in Chatrie v. United States . Through geofencing, tech companies and law enforcement can map everyone who was present within a specific area over a certain window of time, inverting standard constitutional protections by turning every innocent bystander into a potential suspect. While the Supreme Court's ruling in Chatrie established that accessing location data via geofencing constitutes a Fourth Amendment search requiring constitutional protections, law enforcement demands via these warrants are only part of the problem. That same geolocation tracking is used by commercial data brokers operating in a largely unregulated market . These brokers regularly harvest, aggregate, and sell physical location data to anyone with a credit card (including government agencies, which are among their regular clients ). Especially for individuals seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care , attending a protest , or visiting an immigration law clinic, this pervasive commercial location surveillance represents an immediate threat. stories.summary: This post is adapted from a video recorded by EFF and the Trevor Project. Head over to our TikTok or Instagram to watch! EFF answers all the queer digital rights questions you submit to us through our LGBT Q&A . You asked us: What’s one thing I can do today to improve my safety and security online as an LGBTQ+ person? And for this question, we’ve brought in our friends from the Trevor Project to answer together: Hi, I’m Tommy from the Trevor Project ! The Trevor Project’s mission is to end suicide among lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and questioning (LGBTQ+) young people. Our vision is to create a world where all LGBTQ+ young people see a bright future for themselves. EFF and the Trevor Project know that digital security and online safety can feel overwhelming, especially because we all have different levels of concern for different parts of our online lives. Some might be focused on the dangers of doxxing, another might only want to ensure they're not outed. And queer people can be particularly vulnerable to these kinds of online threats. This might seem like a big task, but the one way you can do today to protect yourself is to revise the information you’ve shared with services and platforms to ensure you’re as in control of your information and data as possible: Protect Your Personal Information Be cautious about sharing sensitive details like your full name, address, school, phone number, and personal photos as it might expose identifying information you want to keep private. Consider using an avatar as your profile picture to avoid sharing your personal photos if that makes you more comfortable. Keep it lowkey when talking about work stuff or sharing details about where you’re studying. stories.summary: Five-day showcase reveals leaps Beijing has made in humanoid tech, but also its limitations as US rivals come up from the rear With exploding pelvises, enough comic pratfalls for a Buster Keaton show reel and the odd moment of ruthless violence, the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing gripped the world this week with an unsettling mixture of hilarity, trepidation and relief. The five-day showcase staked out China’s claim to undisputed leadership in humanoid robotics as android martial artists landed knockout roundhouse kicks and robot teams marched into the arena heralded by flag-waving captains astride giant robotic dogs. The games’ blue-riband event, the 100m, did not disappoint when the robot-sprinters ran quicker than Usain Bolt before slamming mindlessly into a padded wall in a blaze of sparks, flames and flying mechanical limbs.
